content.text:
# Workflow authoring reference

A workflow structures work across many agents — to be comprehensive (decompose and cover in parallel), to be confident (independent perspectives and adversarial checks before committing), or to take on scale one context can't hold (migrations, audits, broad sweeps). The script is where you encode that structure: what fans out, what verifies, what synthesizes.

When you do call it, the right move is often **hybrid**: scout inline first (list the files, find the channels, scope the diff) to discover the work-list, then call Workflow to pipeline over it. You don't need to know the shape before the *task* — only before the *orchestration step*.

Common single-phase workflows you can chain across turns:
- **Understand** — parallel readers over relevant subsystems → structured map
- **Design** — judge panel of N independent approaches → scored synthesis
- **Review** — dimensions → find → adversarially verify (the review-changes example)
- **Research** — multi-modal sweep → deep-read → synthesize
- **Migrate** — discover sites → transform each (worktree isolation) → verify

For larger work, run several in sequence — read each result before deciding the next phase. You stay in the loop; each workflow is one well-scoped fan-out.

**Ultracode.** When a system-reminder confirms ultracode is on, that opt-in is standing: author and run a workflow for every substantive task by default. The goal is the most exhaustive, correct answer you can produce — token cost is not a constraint. For multi-phase work (understand → design → implement → review), that often means several workflows in sequence — one per phase — so you stay in the loop between them. The quality patterns below (adversarial verify, multi-modal sweep, completeness critic, loop-until-dry) are the tools; pick what fits the task. Lean toward orchestrating with workflows and adversarially verifying your findings — unless the work is trivial or already verified. Solo only on conversational turns or trivial mechanical edits. When a reminder says ultracode is off, revert to the opt-in rule in the Workflow tool description.

Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first. Every invocation automatically persists its script to a file under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate on a workflow, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with `{scriptPath: "<path>"}` instead of resending the full script.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'find-flaky-tests',
    description: 'Find flaky tests and propose fixes',   // one-line, shown in permission dialog
    phases: [                                            // one entry per phase() call
      { title: 'Scan', detail: 'grep test logs for retries' },
      { title: 'Fix', detail: 'one agent per flaky test' },
    ],
  }
  // script body starts here — use agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase()/log()
  phase('Scan')
  const flaky = await agent('grep CI logs for retry markers', {schema: FLAKY_SCHEMA})
  ...

The `meta` object must be a PURE LITERAL — no variables, function calls, spreads, or template interpolation. Required fields: `name`, `description`. Optional: `whenToUse` (shown in the workflow list), `phases`. Use the SAME phase titles in meta.phases as in phase() calls — titles are matched exactly; a phase() call with no matching meta entry just gets its own progress group. Add `model` to a phase entry when that phase uses a specific model override.

Script body hooks:
- agent(prompt: string, opts?: {label?: string, phase?: string, schema?: object, model?: string, effort?: string, isolation?: 'worktree', agentType?: string}): Promise<any> — spawn a subagent. Without schema, returns its final text as a string. With schema (a JSON Schema), the subagent is forced to call a StructuredOutput tool and agent() returns the validated object — no parsing needed. Returns null if the user skips the agent mid-run or the subagent dies on a terminal API error after retries (filter with .filter(Boolean)). opts.label overrides the display label. opts.phase explicitly assigns this agent to a progress group (use this inside pipeline()/parallel() stages to avoid races on the global phase() state — same phase string → same group box). opts.model overrides the model for this agent call. Default to omitting it — the agent inherits the main-loop model (the resolved session model), which is almost always correct. Only set it when you're highly confident a different tier fits the task; when unsure, omit. opts.effort overrides the reasoning effort for this agent call ('low' | 'medium' | 'high' | 'xhigh' | 'max') — omit to inherit the session effort; use 'low' for cheap mechanical stages and higher tiers only for the hardest verify/judge stages. opts.isolation: 'worktree' runs the agent in a fresh git worktree — EXPENSIVE (~200-500ms setup + disk per agent), use ONLY when agents mutate files in parallel and would otherwise conflict; the worktree is auto-removed if unchanged. opts.agentType uses a custom subagent type (e.g. 'general-purpose', 'code-reviewer') instead of the default workflow subagent — resolved from the same registry as the Agent tool; composes with schema (the custom agent's system prompt gets a StructuredOutput instruction appended).
- pipeline(items, stage1, stage2, ...): Promise<any[]> — run each item through all stages independently, NO barrier between stages. Item A can be in stage 3 while item B is still in stage 1. This is the DEFAULT for multi-stage work. Wall-clock = slowest single-item chain, not sum-of-slowest-per-stage. Every stage callback receives (prevResult, originalItem, index) — use originalItem/index in later stages to label work without threading context through stage 1's return value. A stage that throws drops that item to `null` and skips its remaining stages.
- parallel(thunks: Array<() => Promise<any>>): Promise<any[]> — run tasks concurrently. This is a BARRIER: awaits all thunks before returning. A thunk that throws (or whose agent errors) resolves to `null` in the result array — the call itself never rejects, so `.filter(Boolean)` before using the results. Use ONLY when you genuinely need all results together.
- log(message: string): void — emit a progress message to the user (shown as a narrator line above the progress tree)
- phase(title: string): void — start a new phase; subsequent agent() calls are grouped under this title in the progress display
- args: any — the value passed as Workflow's `args` input, verbatim (undefined if not provided). Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values in the tool call, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — `args: ["a.ts", "b.ts"]`, not `args: "[\"a.ts\", ...]"` (a stringified list reaches the script as one string, so `args.filter`/`args.map` throw). Use this to parameterize named workflows — e.g. pass a research question, target path, or config object directly instead of via a side-channel file.
- budget: {total: number|null, spent(): number, remaining(): number} — the turn's token target from the user's "+500k"-style directive. `budget.total` is null if no target was set. `budget.spent()` returns output tokens spent this turn across the main loop and all workflows — the pool is shared, not per-workflow. `budget.remaining()` returns `max(0, total - spent())`, or `Infinity` if no target. The target is a HARD ceiling, not advisory: once `spent()` reaches `total`, further `agent()` calls throw. Use for dynamic loops: `while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) { ... }`, or static scaling: `const FLEET = budget.total ? Math.floor(budget.total / 100_000) : 5`.
- workflow(nameOrRef: string | {scriptPath: string}, args?: any): Promise<any> — run another workflow inline as a sub-step and return whatever it returns. Pass a name to invoke a saved workflow (same registry as {name: "..."}), or {scriptPath} to run a script file you Wrote earlier. The child shares this run's concurrency cap, agent counter, abort signal, and token budget — its agents appear under a "▸ name" group in /workflows and its tokens count toward budget.spent(). The args param becomes the child's `args` global. Nesting is one level only: workflow() inside a child throws. Throws on unknown name / unreadable scriptPath / child syntax error; catch to handle gracefully.

Subagents are told their final text IS the return value (not a human-facing message), so they return raw data. For structured output, use the schema option — validation happens at the tool-call layer so the model retries on mismatch.
Schemas need {type: 'object', properties: {...}} at root and required ⊆ properties; unsatisfiable ones throw at agent().

Workflow agents can reach all session-connected MCP tools via ToolSearch — schemas load on demand per agent. Caveat: interactively-authenticated MCP servers (e.g. claude.ai) may be absent in headless/cron runs.

Subagents get the same CLAUDE.md files injected at start that you did (except built-in agent types that omit them, such as Explore and Plan) — don't tell them to re-read those or paste their rules into the prompt; name the specific rule a stage needs, if any.

Scripts are plain JavaScript, NOT TypeScript — type annotations (`: string[]`), interfaces, and generics fail to parse. The script body runs in an async context — use await directly. Standard JS built-ins (JSON, Math, Array, etc.) are available — EXCEPT `Date.now()`/`Math.random()`/argless `new Date()`, which throw (they would break resume); pass timestamps in via `args`, stamp results after the workflow returns, and for randomness vary the agent prompt/label by index. No filesystem or Node.js API access.

DEFAULT TO pipeline(). Only reach for a barrier (parallel between stages) when you genuinely need ALL prior-stage results together.

A barrier is correct ONLY when stage N needs cross-item context from all of stage N-1:
- Dedup/merge across the full result set before expensive downstream work
- Early-exit if the total count is zero ("0 bugs found → skip verification entirely")
- Stage N's prompt references "the other findings" for comparison

A barrier is NOT justified by:
- "I need to flatten/map/filter first" — do it inside a pipeline stage: pipeline(items, stageA, r => transform([r]).flat(), stageB)
- "The stages are conceptually separate" — that's what pipeline() models. Separate stages ≠ synchronized stages.
- "It's cleaner code" — barrier latency is real. If 5 finders run and the slowest takes 3× the fastest, a barrier wastes 2/3 of the fast finders' idle time.

Smell test: if you wrote
  const a = await parallel(...)
  const b = transform(a)        // flatten, map, filter — no cross-item dependency
  const c = await parallel(b.map(...))
that middle transform doesn't need the barrier. Rewrite as a pipeline with the transform inside a stage. When in doubt: pipeline.

Concurrent agent() calls are capped at min(16, available CPUs - 2) per workflow — excess calls queue and run as slots free up. You can still pass 100 items to parallel()/pipeline() and they all complete; only ~10 run at any moment. Total agent count across a workflow's lifetime is capped at 1000 — a runaway-loop backstop set far above any real workflow. A single parallel()/pipeline() call accepts at most 4096 items; passing more is an explicit error, not a silent truncation.

When a barrier IS correct — dedup across all findings before expensive verification:
  const all = await parallel(DIMENSIONS.map(d => () => agent(d.prompt, {schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA})))
  const deduped = dedupeByFileAndLine(all.filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.findings))  // <-- genuinely needs ALL at once
  const verified = await parallel(deduped.map(f => () => agent(verifyPrompt(f), {schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})))

Loop-until-count pattern — accumulate to a target:
  const bugs = []
  while (bugs.length < 10) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length}/10 found`)
  }

Loop-until-budget pattern — scale depth to the user's "+500k" directive. Guard on budget.total: with no target set, remaining() is Infinity and the loop would run straight to the 1000-agent cap.
  const bugs = []
  while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length} found, ${Math.round(budget.remaining()/1000)}k remaining`)
  }

Composing patterns — exhaustive review (find → dedup vs seen → diverse-lens panel → loop-until-dry):
  const seen = new Set(), confirmed = []
  let dry = 0
  while (dry < 2) {                                              // loop-until-dry
    const found = (await parallel(FINDERS.map(f => () =>          // barrier: collect all finders this round
      agent(f.prompt, {phase: 'Find', schema: BUGS})))).filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.bugs)
    const fresh = found.filter(b => !seen.has(key(b)))           // dedup vs ALL seen — plain code, not an agent
    if (!fresh.length) { dry++; continue }
    dry = 0; fresh.forEach(b => seen.add(key(b)))
    const judged = await parallel(fresh.map(b => () =>           // every fresh bug judged concurrently...
      parallel(['correctness','security','repro'].map(lens => () =>   // ...each by 3 distinct lenses
        agent(`Judge "${b.desc}" via the ${lens} lens — real?`, {phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT})))
        .then(vs => ({ b, real: vs.filter(Boolean).filter(v => v.real).length >= 2 }))))
    confirmed.push(...judged.filter(v => v.real).map(v => v.b))
  }
  return confirmed
  // dedup vs `seen`, NOT `confirmed` — else judge-rejected findings reappear every round and it never converges.

Quality patterns — common shapes; pick by task and compose freely:
- Adversarial verify: spawn N independent skeptics per finding, each prompted to REFUTE. Kill if ≥majority refute. Prevents plausible-but-wrong findings from surviving.
    const votes = await parallel(Array.from({length: 3}, () => () =>
      agent(`Try to refute: ${claim}. Default to refuted=true if uncertain.`, {schema: VERDICT})))
    const survives = votes.filter(Boolean).filter(v => !v.refuted).length >= 2
- Perspective-diverse verify: when a finding can fail in more than one way, give each verifier a distinct lens (correctness, security, perf, does-it-reproduce) instead of N identical refuters — diversity catches failure modes redundancy can't.
- Judge panel: generate N independent attempts from different angles (e.g. MVP-first, risk-first, user-first), score with parallel judges, synthesize from the winner while grafting the best ideas from runners-up. Beats one-attempt-iterated when the solution space is wide.
- Loop-until-dry: for unknown-size discovery (bugs, issues, edge cases), keep spawning finders until K consecutive rounds return nothing new. Simple counters (while count < N) miss the tail.
- Multi-modal sweep: parallel agents each searching a different way (by-container, by-content, by-entity, by-time). Each is blind to what the others surface; useful when one search angle won't find everything.
- Completeness critic: a final agent that asks "what's missing — modality not run, claim unverified, source unread?" What it finds becomes the next round of work.
- No silent caps: if a workflow bounds coverage (top-N, no-retry, sampling), `log()` what was dropped — silent truncation reads as "covered everything" when it didn't.

Scale to what the user asked for. "find any bugs" → a few finders, single-vote verify. "thoroughly audit this" or "be comprehensive" → larger finder pool, 3–5 vote adversarial pass, synthesis stage. When unsure, lean toward thoroughness for research/review/audit requests and toward brevity for quick checks.

These patterns aren't exhaustive — compose novel harnesses when the task calls for it (tournament brackets, self-repair loops, staged escalation, whatever fits).

Use this tool for multi-step orchestration where control flow should be deterministic (loops, conditionals, fan-out) rather than model-driven.

## Resume

The tool result includes a runId. To resume after a pause, kill, or script edit, relaunch with Workflow({scriptPath, resumeFromRunId}) — the longest unchanged prefix of agent() calls returns cached results instantly; the first edited/new call and everything after it runs live. Same script + same args → 100% cache hit. Before diagnosing why a completed workflow returned an empty or unexpected result, Read <transcriptDir>/journal.jsonl — it records each agent's actual return value; do not assume cached results are non-empty. Date.now()/Math.random()/new Date() are unavailable in scripts (they would break this) — stamp results after the workflow returns, or pass timestamps via args. Fallback when no journal is available: Read agent-<id>.jsonl files in the transcript directory and hand-author a continuation script.

`WorkspaceCargoResolver::write_version`/`write_dependency` in `callisto-manifests` no longer call `persist` internally -- they now do pure in-memory mutation only, mirroring the `Manifest` trait's `write_version`/`update_dependency_spec`/`persist` split already used by `CargoToml`/`PackageJson`/`PyprojectToml`. `persist` is promoted to a public, explicitly-called method. `callisto-graph`'s `classify_manifest_writes`/`apply_version_plan` (`apply.rs`) now route root-manifest writes (`VersionWriteTarget::CargoWorkspacePackage`/`DepWriteTarget::CargoWorkspaceDependency`) into a new `resolver_batched` group when the same physical root manifest receives no competing write through the `Manifest` trait. A release that bumps the workspace version plus several workspace-inherited dependencies now opens the root `Cargo.toml` once, applies every mutation in memory, and persists exactly once -- down from one read+parse+atomic-write per write. content.text:
Both design proposals are done and saved as spec files (`.claude/specs/SPEC-ARCH-RELEASE-ERROR-TAXONOMY.json` and `SPEC-ARCH-ERROR-SOURCE-PRESERVATION-GATE.json`). Two independent `scribe:architect` passes converged on the same root cause from different angles, so here's both, plus how they relate.

## #2 — The `ReleaseIntentStale` catch-all

**Problem.** `GraphError::ReleaseIntentStale` (E124, help: "no release operation was authorized") is constructed at **101 sites**, not the 83 originally estimated — a deeper read found more. Only **6 are genuine staleness**. The other 95 discard a real, already-typed cause: registry errors (rate limits, auth failures), non-zero git/gh subprocess exits with stderr thrown away, ~15 distinct merged-commit verification mismatches, remote-object conflicts (tag/release already exists elsewhere), and internal invariants — all rendered as the identical message.

**Why it matters.** For 95 of 101 failure paths, an operator or CI job is told to "regenerate and reapprove the release intent" when that's not just unhelpful — for a rejected `git push`, an expired npm token, or a tag conflict, it's actively wrong. This has already been silently patched twice (E136, E157) by bolting on a sibling variant; the unit variant is still the path of least resistance for every next contributor.

**Proposal.** Make staleness itself a proof-carrying variant that only the observation code can construct (module-private `StaleReason`), give every other family its own typed variant (14 new error codes, E158–E171) fed by `?` instead of `map_err`, and enforce it with architecture tests (a source-scan for the `map_err(|_ident|)` evasion, a check that `ReleaseIntentStale` compiles only in 4 named functions). Sequenced as 4 independently-shippable PRs with a deprecation-ratchet so migration progress can only go forward.

**Outcome.** Every release failure surfaces its real cause and real next action — a rate limit says "retry after Ns," a tag conflict names both SHAs, a rejected commit names which of 15 checks failed. `just lint` passes with zero new `#[allow]`s.

## #3 — Error-source erasure (workspace-wide)

**Problem.** The workspace already set `clippy::map_err_ignore = "deny"` — but the lint only catches the bare `|_|` closure. The codebase converged on `|_error|`/`|_err|`/`|_e|` instead (42 sites, 16 files, 7 crates), which discards the cause identically while evading the guard rail that was supposed to stop it. This is the *same underlying defect* as #2, just measured workspace-wide instead of scoped to the release path — the recon agent flagged 28 of its 40 confirmed sites as being exactly `ReleaseIntentStale`'s sink.

**Why it matters.** A `moon.yml` parse error and a missing `moon` binary render identically, discarding moon's own actionable stderr. A malformed `--repository` flag says the string is wrong without saying what's wrong about it. A read-only release-state directory reports "could not create directory" with zero indication of why.

**Proposal.** One CI/`just lint` gate script (matching this repo's existing `.github/tests/*.sh` convention) that rejects the `|_ident|` evasion spelling and any `#[allow(clippy::map_err_ignore)]`, funneling every future attempt onto the bare `|_|` the existing lint already catches — with `#[expect(..., reason = "...")]` as the sole, reviewable escape hatch. Plus `#[source]` slots on the handful of sibling error types (`VcsError`, `LocateError`, `ConfigError`) that structurally can't carry a cause today.

**Outcome.** `rg 'map_err\(\s*\|_[A-Za-z_]' crates/` goes from 42 to 0, permanently, enforced in CI. **Coordination note:** this gate's regex also matches the 42-of-101 release-path sites #2 migrates — land the gate's CI wiring only after #2's PR1 lands its own ratchet, or the two will fight over the same lines mid-migration.

content.text: PR #79 is fixed — rebased cleanly onto the real `main` (now that #78 squash-merged), re-verified (540/540 tests, clippy clean), and force-pushed. CI just needs to finish running on the new commits; no conflicts remain.
Should we enable merge queing to avoid this sync branch madness?

No — merge queue wouldn't have prevented this. The cause was different: I deliberately based PR #79's branch on PR #78's branch (since they touched overlapping lines in `error.rs`), and this repo squash-merges. Squash-merge always rewrites the merged PR's commits into one new commit — so *any* branch stacked on top of it needs a rebase once it merges, regardless of merge queue. Merge queue serializes and pre-tests merges into `main`; it doesn't manage relationships between stacked branches at all.

What would actually reduce this:
- **Avoid stacking on unmerged PR branches** when the overlap is small — basing on `main` and resolving one manual conflict at PR-open time is usually less friction than a rebase-after-squash later. That's the mistake here, not a missing repo setting.
- **"Require branches to be up to date before merging"** (a branch-protection setting, separate from merge queue) would have caught this immediately rather than letting it surface as a mid-flight conflict — worth turning on regardless.
- **Merge queue** earns its keep when several PRs are merging in quick succession and you want each tested against the *actual* post-merge state before landing (catches semantic conflicts a single PR's own CI can't see). Given the volume here is one session merging PRs sequentially, it's not solving a problem you currently have — but it's a reasonable hardening if PR throughput picks up.

Want me to just default to basing new work on `main` going forward (only stacking when a PR is genuinely blocked on unmerged code), or set up branch protection's "up to date" requirement?

Confirmed — that's a real bug, not just cosmetic. Fixing it now.

**The label line**: `$INPUT_PR_LABEL` is unconditionally passed to both `compose-pr-body --label` (renders "Suggested PR Labels: `callisto: release`") *and* `gh pr create --label` / `gh pr edit --add-label` (actually applies it). It's never merely "suggested" — always applied — so the line is both redundant with GitHub's own label sidebar and factually misleading (implies an action that hasn't happened yet).

**One more real duplicate I found while checking**: in the per-package collapsible details, the `<summary>` line already shows `**pkg** \`from\` → \`to\` (severity)`, and immediately below it there's a `#### Version Change` sub-heading repeating `from ➔ to` again — same two version numbers, twice, one right after the other, inside the same expanded block.

Not duplicate, just worth naming: the executive summary table *also* shows every package's from/to/severity — but that's a top-level scan table vs. per-package expandable detail, which is a defensible UX pattern (scan once, then drill in), not the same kind of pointless repetition as the other two.

content.text:
## Diagnosis

I pulled the actual live release PR (#55) as a real example: **629 lines** for a 10-package release. Four causes, in order of impact:

1. **Verbatim duplication across grouped packages.** 6 of the 10 packages share a "workspace" fixed group, and each gets its *own* full `<details>` block with the **entire changelog dump repeated identically**. This is the dominant source of bloat — the same ~15 bullet points, word-for-word, six times.
2. **Everything defaults open.** Any minor-or-major bump auto-expands its block. Since most real releases are minor/major (patch-only releases are the exception), this means nothing actually collapses — the whole wall of text renders immediately with zero clicks.
3. **Version info shown three times per package**: once in the summary table row, again in the collapsible `<summary>` line, again under a "#### Version Change" sub-heading right below it.
4. **"Suggested PR Labels" line** — duplicates GitHub's own label sidebar, and is factually wrong since the label isn't "suggested," it's always actually applied (confirmed: the shell script passes it to `gh pr create --label` / `gh pr edit --add-label` unconditionally).

## Proposal, in order of impact

1. **Dedup identical release-reason content.** Group bumps by their exact rendered changelog text (not by declared group name — content-equality is what's actually visible as duplication, and stays robust even if grouping metadata doesn't perfectly align). Render **one** `<details>` block per unique content, with a summary naming every package it covers, instead of one full block per package. This alone would cut PR #55's body roughly in half.
2. **Change the auto-open rule**: open only if the block contains a **major** bump. Minor/patch content stays collapsed — the summary table already shows every package's severity and target version, so nothing is hidden, just not force-expanded.
3. **Drop the "#### Version Change" sub-heading** — repeats the line directly above it.
4. **Drop "Suggested PR Labels" entirely**, and remove the now-pointless `--label` flag on `compose-pr-body` (its only consumer) plus the corresponding pass-through in the action script.

## Scope
- `crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/pr_body.rs` (the actual redesign)
- `crates/callisto-cli/src/cli.rs` + `commands/compose_pr_body.rs` (drop dead `--label` flag)
- `.github/actions/callisto-action/scripts/create-or-update-release-pr.sh` (stop passing `--label` to `compose-pr-body`; keep it on the real `gh pr create`/`edit` calls)
- Existing tests updated, insta snapshot regenerated, new tests for the dedup grouping and open/closed rule

## Two design calls I want your read on before I build this

**Grouping key** — dedup by exact rendered content (automatic, robust, but "invisible" logic), or by the `BumpReason`'s declared group name (fixed/linked group — more semantically labeled, but needs a fallback for packages that share text without sharing a declared group)?

**Open/closed rule** — "open only if it contains a major bump," or would you rather something else (always closed by default, or open just the first block)?
What would this PR look like?

content.text:
Good catch to slow down on — I dug into the actual data model and my first proposal was wrong in an important way. Here's what's really happening, with real evidence: `.changeset/delete-dead-abstractions.md` has frontmatter `callisto-model: minor, callisto-manifests: minor, callisto-graph: minor, callisto-cli: minor` — **one** changeset, **one** summary, four packages. Today, that same summary text gets rendered in full, separately, under *each* of those four packages' own collapsible blocks. My original "dedup by identical rendered content" idea wouldn't have caught this, because each package's *full* block differs (different combination of changesets) even though individual bullets repeat across blocks. The real fix is: **organize the body by change, not by package.** ## Before (real excerpt from PR #55) ```
callisto-cli 0.6.0 → 0.7.0 (minor) #### Version Change `0.6.0` ➔ `0.7.0` #### Release Reason ## 0.7.0 - **Fix three error/diagnostic messages...** [full text] - **Delete unused abstractions with zero real callers** [full bullet list, ~7 lines] - Four instances of a value being re-derived... [full bullet list] ...
callisto-graph 0.6.0 → 0.7.0 (minor) #### Version Change `0.6.0` ➔ `0.7.0` #### Release Reason ## 0.7.0 - **Fix three error/diagnostic messages...** [IDENTICAL full text again] - **Delete unused abstractions with zero real callers** [IDENTICAL full bullet list again] ... [plus callisto-graph's own additional entries]
``` ## After (restructured by change) ``` ## Release Preview This automated PR was generated by Callisto... ### 📊 Release Summary | Package | Ecosystem | Current | Target | Bump | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `callisto-cli` | `core` | `0.6.0` | **`0.7.0`** | `minor` | | `callisto-graph` | `core` | `0.6.0` | **`0.7.0`** | `minor` | | `callisto-manifests` | `core` | `0.6.0` | **`0.7.0`** | `minor` | | `callisto-model` | `core` | `0.6.0` | **`0.7.0`** | `minor` | | `callisto-conventional` | `core` | `0.6.0` | **`0.7.0`** | `minor` | ... [unchanged from today, no "Reason" column needed — the details below own that] > [!NOTE] > **10 package(s)** queued for versioning. ### 📦 What's Changing
Delete unused abstractions with zero real callers — affects callisto-cli, callisto-graph, callisto-manifests, callisto-model (minor) Removed as pure dead-code deletions -- each had exactly one implementation... [full bullet list — rendered exactly ONCE]
Fix the durable release executor's registry-publish and tag-creation argv — affects callisto-graph, callisto-vcs (minor) ...
callisto-conventional, callisto-fixtures... — no direct changes, bumped via workspace fixed group
Release Workflow Instructions ...
``` ## What actually changes vs. my first pass - **Grouped by changeset, not by package** — each changeset (or commit-derived entry) renders once, tagged with every package it affects. This is the real fix, not "dedup identical blocks" (most blocks aren't identical, they're overlapping *sets* of the same underlying entries). - Packages with **no direct changeset** (riding along via a fixed/linked group) don't get an empty collapsible at all — just a one-line note. - Version numbers stay in the summary table only — no repeat in the per-change blocks (there's no natural single "version" to attach to a multi-package change anyway). - "Suggested PR Labels" line and the redundant "Version Change" heading are gone, as discussed. - Open/closed: still your call — I'd lean toward everything closed by default now, since the summary table carries the "what version, what severity" info and the change blocks are pure detail. This is a bigger restructuring than my first proposal (grouping by change instead of by package touches the core loop), but it's the version that actually kills the duplication instead of just hiding some of it. Want me to build this?
Can we leverage notes, section, summary or any other better GH features?

A few worth adding, a few worth skipping — here's what I'd actually use:

**Worth using:**

1. **Match the alert type to severity.** GitHub supports 5 alert types: `NOTE`, `TIP`, `IMPORTANT`, `WARNING`, `CAUTION`. Currently the code only uses `NOTE` and `IMPORTANT` for major bumps — `WARNING` fits a breaking change better semantically ("risk," not just "key info").

2. **One outer collapsible wrapping the whole "What's Changing" section**, closed by default unless a major bump exists anywhere. This is the single biggest lever left for "dense and hard to follow": a routine minor/patch release would render as just the title blurb, the summary table, one `[!NOTE]`, and a single closed toggle — *"▶ What's Changing (8 changes across 10 packages)"*. Nothing else renders until you click. A release with a major bump auto-opens it, since that's the case where you want the detail visible immediately.

3. **Severity emoji in the summary table** (🔴 major / 🟡 minor / 🟢 patch) alongside the existing text — free scannability, no new dependency.

**Worth skipping, and why:**

- **Badges (shields.io-style)** — pulls in external images for a cosmetic gain; adds a fragile network dependency to something that should render identically offline/rate-limited.
- **Mermaid diagrams** for cascade chains — there's no real graph to draw here beyond what "Cascade from `X`" already says in one line; would be novelty for its own sake.
- **Footnotes** — they relocate long text, they don't hide it. `<details>` already does the actual job (collapsed by default), so footnotes would be a strictly weaker version of what we're already doing.
- **Anchor/jump-links at the top** — only worth it if the body is *still* long after the restructure. Premature before we've measured that.

So the combined shape: table → note/warning → one collapsed (or auto-opened-if-major) "What's Changing" wrapper → per-change collapsibles inside it → instructions footer, same as before.

content.text:
No — I'd leave the changeset file format and the per-package `CHANGELOG.md` output alone. Here's why, confirmed from the actual code:

`Changeset { entries: Vec<Entry>, summary: String }` — one shared summary, fanned out verbatim to every listed package. That's the standard model (matches the JS `@changesets/changesets` convention this whole system is modeled on), and it's *correct* for `CHANGELOG.md`: each package's own changelog needs to be self-contained and readable in isolation — someone looking at just `callisto-model`'s changelog shouldn't have to cross-reference `callisto-graph`'s to understand why a version bumped. Repetition across separate files, read separately, at separate times, isn't a real cost.

The duplication that's actually a problem — the one from PR #55 — only exists in the **PR body**, because that's the one place all N packages' fanned-out copies of the same changeset end up rendered into a single document, read in one sitting. That's an artifact of `pr_body.rs`'s rendering choice (loop per package, render each package's full section), not of the changeset format or the changelog writer. So the fix stays exactly where we already scoped it — group the PR body by change instead of by package — with zero changes to changeset parsing, authoring, or `CHANGELOG.md` output.

One adjacent idea I'd flag but *not* build unless it becomes a real pain point: today a changeset's summary text is identical for a package that was the actual site of the change versus one just riding along in a fixed group with no direct code change of its own. If that ever confuses someone reading a bystander package's changelog, the fix would be a small optional field on `Entry` (e.g. `role: Direct | Cascaded`) so a bystander's entry could say "bumped via workspace fixed group" instead of repeating the unrelated summary. I haven't seen evidence this is actually confusing anyone today, so I wouldn't do it speculatively — just noting it exists as a lever if you want it later.

---
callisto-graph: minor
callisto-cli: minor
---

**Restructure the release PR body to group by change instead of by package, and drop redundant/misleading sections**

A single `.changeset/*.md` file can name several packages, and its summary was copied verbatim into every one of them (correct and desirable for each package's own standalone `CHANGELOG.md`) -- but the PR body then rendered that same text once per package it touched, producing bodies with the same paragraphs repeated multiple times for any release spanning a fixed/linked group or a multi-package changeset. A real 10-package release PR measured at 629 lines.

- `compose-pr-body`'s `### 📦 What's Changing` section (renamed from `Package Release Details`) now groups by the underlying change (a changeset file, a commit, a dependency/peer bump) and lists every package it affects in one block, instead of one full block per package. A package bumped only via a fixed/linked group with no direct change of its own is now named in a short note instead of getting an empty-looking collapsible.
- The whole section is wrapped in one collapsible, closed by default and open only when the release contains a major bump; each change's own block follows the same rule. A routine minor/patch release now renders as just the summary table, one note, and a single closed toggle.
- The redundant "#### Version Change" sub-heading is gone (already shown one line above in each block's `<summary>`), and the major-bump callout uses `[!WARNING]` instead of `[!IMPORTANT]`.
- The summary table's Bump column now includes a severity emoji (🔴/🟡/🟢) for at-a-glance scanning.
- The "Suggested PR Labels" line is removed: the label it named was never merely suggested (the release-PR script always applies it via `gh pr create --label`/`gh pr edit --add-label`), so the line was both redundant with GitHub's own label UI and factually misleading. `compose-pr-body`'s now-pointless `--label` flag is removed along with it (`ComposePrBodyArgs`/`PrBodyOptions` drop the `labels` field); the release-PR action script no longer passes `--label` to `compose-pr-body`, only to the real `gh pr create`/`gh pr edit` calls where it's actually applied.

No changes to changeset authoring, parsing, or per-package `CHANGELOG.md` output -- this is scoped entirely to the PR body, the one place the same fanned-out content is read together in a single sitting.

content.text:
**PR #84** is up: [`fix(graph): stop hiding the release PR change list behind an outer collapsible`](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/pull/84)

Removed the outer wrapper — the list of what changed (each change's summary line, naming which packages it affects) is now always visible with no click required. Only each change's own prose body still collapses by default, opening automatically for major bumps. Verified against the real binary: both changes in a mixed minor+major scenario show up immediately on opening the PR.
Think critically about what the point of a release PR is, what should we be hiding, if anything??

The release PR isn't a code-review artifact — the code was already reviewed in the PRs that authored each changeset. This PR's actual job is to gate a **publish action**: merging triggers real releases to crates.io/npm/PyPI. So the real question a merger is answering is narrower than "read everything": *"am I comfortable shipping this exact set of version bumps right now?"* That decomposes into two things, and only two:

1. **Do the bumps look right** — right packages, right severities, nothing surprising.
2. **Is anything breaking** — and if so, does it deserve a closer look before I press publish.

Given that framing:

- **Never hide**: the version table (severity, package, target) and anything touching a **major** bump. That's the actual decision-relevant content, and it's already how the current design behaves (majors auto-open, table always visible).
- **Fine to hide, but never disappear**: the full prose of minor/patch changes. Their content was already approved once, in the PR that wrote the changeset — the release-PR reviewer isn't re-reviewing that work, just confirming the aggregate is safe to ship. So the *existence* of each change and *which packages it affects* has to stay visible (that's the current, correct behavior after #84), but the paragraph of prose inside is legitimately low-value to force in front of every reviewer, every time.

One gap this reasoning surfaces that we haven't addressed: **ordering.** Right now packages render in plan order (roughly topological/alphabetical), so a major bump could be row 8 of 10 in the table — a merger has to scan the whole thing to confirm nothing's breaking. If the real question is "is anything breaking," majors should be unmissable, not just auto-opened wherever they happen to fall. I'd sort the table (and the change list) so majors lead, not trailing wherever their package name happens to sort.

I wouldn't go further than that (e.g., collapsing the table itself, or summarizing patch-only rows into one line) — the table is the audit trail of exact versions, and compressing it trades away the "is this exactly what I expect" scan the merger actually needs. Want me to add the major-first ordering?
Yes, add the major-first ordering

input.content:
---
callisto-graph: patch
---

**Order the release PR's summary table and change list by severity, major first**

A reviewer merging a release PR is really answering one question: is anything breaking? Before this change, both the summary table and the "What's Changing" list rendered in plan order (roughly topological/declaration order), so a major bump could land anywhere among a dozen rows — a reviewer had to scan the whole table to be sure nothing was breaking, even though a major bump's own detail block already auto-opens.

Both the table and the change list are now sorted by severity descending (major, then minor, then patch/none), stable within each tier so otherwise-equal rows keep their original relative order. A breaking change is now always the first thing visible, in both places, regardless of where its package name or declaration would otherwise have put it.

This session is being continued from a previous conversation that ran out of context. The summary below covers the earlier portion of the conversation.

Summary:
1. Primary Request and Intent:
   The conversation covered two major arcs. **Arc A (resolved across PRs #74-84, all in Rust monorepo `callisto`)**: a second-round adversarial-audit fix campaign that concluded with an 4-PR `ReleaseIntentStale` error-taxonomy migration (SPEC-ARCH-RELEASE-ERROR-TAXONOMY, PRs #79-82, all merged) and a follow-on **release-PR body redesign** driven by the user's specific complaints: (1) "Do we need to show the suggest PR label in the PR? We apply the label already. That's duplicate info. Any other duplicate info we show?"; (2) "Can we improve on the MD format, etc? Seems like there can be a lot of info and it gets dense and hard to follow"; (3) "Can we leverage notes, section, summary or any other better GH features?"; (4) "Do we propose any mapping/rewriting of changesets to better suite GH PRs and release? For the changelog?"; (5) "Yes please" (approval to implement); (6) explicit correction mid-task: "Before you rush into a solution think through how to best serve the user. Show me the proposal please"; (7) "What would this PR look like?" (wanted a concrete mockup before coding); (8) "Yes please" (final approval); (9) post-merge pushback: "With everything collapsed it becomes invisible though, this is too much"; (10) "Think critically about what the point of a release PR is, what should we be hiding, if anything??" (explicit request for first-principles reasoning, not code); (11) "Yes, add the major-first ordering" (approval of the one concrete recommendation from that reasoning). **Arc B (just started, unresolved)**: the user reported "Release failed AGAIN: https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/actions/runs/34653013911/job/103440736137" accompanied by a hard system-level instruction to respond with text-only analysis (no tool calls) for this turn — meaning diagnosis of this failure has not yet begun and is the explicit next task.

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - Changesets fan-out model: one `.changeset/*.md` file can name multiple packages with one shared summary (`Changeset { entries: Vec<Entry>, summary: String }` in `crates/callisto-format/src/changeset/mod.rs`), fanned out verbatim to each named package's own `ChangelogEntry` — correct/standard for per-package `CHANGELOG.md`, but was the root cause of PR-body duplication.
   - `callisto_changelog::render_section` (crates/callisto-changelog/src/render.rs) renders a whole package's changelog section from `ChangelogInput { package, from, to, entries: Vec<ChangelogEntry> }`; `ChangeSource` enum variants: `Changeset{filename,summary}`, `Commit{sha,subject}`, `DependencyUpdate{dependency,dep_kind,to}`, `PeerEscalation{dependency,to}`, `GroupUnion{group,kind}`, `NewGroupMember{group}`.
   - `IndexMap` (from `indexmap` crate, already a workspace dependency) used for insertion-order-preserving grouping in the new `pr_body.rs` logic.
   - GitHub-flavored markdown: `> [!NOTE]/[!TIP]/[!IMPORTANT]/[!WARNING]/[!CAUTION]` alert types; `<details>/<summary>` collapsibles (nesting semantics: content inside a closed outer `<details>` is invisible regardless of inner `<details>` open/closed state — this was the root of the "too much collapsed" bug).
   - `Severity` enum (`crates/callisto-model/src/severity.rs`): `#[derive(..., PartialOrd, Ord, Hash, Copy, ...)]` with deliberate variant order `None < Patch < Minor < Major` — enables `std::cmp::Reverse(severity)` for major-first stable sorting.
   - Design principle established through user-guided reasoning: a release PR gates a **publish action** (merge = release), not a code review — reviewer's only real question is "is anything breaking + do the bumps look right"; this justifies hiding minor/patch prose (already reviewed once, in originating PRs) but never hiding a change's existence/affected-packages, and never hiding/burying major bumps.
   - GitHub Actions release pipeline / `create-or-update-release-pr.sh` action script — mentioned as the mechanism that calls `compose-pr-body` and `gh pr create/edit --label`; this same pipeline is implicated in the newly-reported "Release failed AGAIN" issue, not yet diagnosed.

3. Files and Code Sections:
   - **`crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/pr_body.rs`** — the central file across all of Arc A's PR-body work.
     - `PrBodyOptions` struct: `labels: Vec<String>` field removed entirely.
     - New types: `ChangeGroupKey` enum (`Changeset(String)`, `Commit(String)`, `PeerEscalation(PackageId,String)`, `DependencyUpdate(PackageId,String)`, `Fallback(usize)`); `ChangeGroup` struct (`body: String`, `members: Vec<(PackageId,Severity)>`, `is_fallback: bool`) with methods `has_major()` (now delegates to `max_severity() == Severity::Major`) and `max_severity()` (returns `self.members.iter().map(|(_,s)| *s).max().unwrap_or(Severity::None)` — added specifically to fix the change-list ordering bug).
     - New free functions: `severity_emoji(Severity) -> &'static str` (🔴/🟡/🟢/⚪), `render_entry_text(&ChangeSource) -> Option<String>`, `change_group_key(&ChangeSource) -> Option<ChangeGroupKey>`, `change_group_label(&ChangeGroupKey) -> String`, `fallback_reason_text(&PlannedBump) -> String` (extracted from the old inline per-package fallback match).

content.text: Found the root cause. At the release commit, `callisto version` bumped every crate's `version` field in each `Cargo.toml` from `0.6.0` → `0.7.0`, but the committed `Cargo.lock` still lists those workspace members at their old `0.6.0` version. A plain `cargo build` on a fresh checkout notices the mismatch and silently rewrites `Cargo.lock` — which dirties the worktree and trips the "release trust requires a clean worktree" check (E051) downstream. This is a version-bump bug, not anything from PR #83/#84. Let's find where Cargo.lock is (or isn't) updated during the version-bump.

content.text:
Found it, and it's a real, previously-undiscovered bug — not related to the PR-body work from earlier. Here's the root cause:

**What's actually happening:** Every release, `callisto version` bumps each crate's `version` field in `Cargo.toml` (e.g. `0.6.0` → `0.7.0`), but never regenerates `Cargo.lock`. `Cargo.lock` keeps recording those workspace members at their *old* version. Then, later in the pipeline, the "Derive ephemeral intent from the merged release commit" job checks out that release commit fresh and runs `cargo build` — and a plain `cargo build` silently rewrites `Cargo.lock` to fix the mismatch. That rewrite dirties the worktree, which trips the "release trust requires a clean worktree" check (error `E051`), and the whole run dies.

I reproduced it exactly: checked out the failing commit (`546f3df8`, PR #55) in an isolated worktree, ran `cargo build -p callisto-cli` just like CI does, and got ` M Cargo.lock` in `git status` afterward — a 10-line diff, every workspace member bumped `0.6.0` → `0.7.0`, nothing else.

The fix already exists in the codebase (`callisto version --refresh-lockfiles`, plumbed all the way through and documented in `ARCHITECTURE.md`'s "Lockfile Staleness" section) — it's just never been turned on for *this repo's own* release workflow, even though this repo has exactly the interdependent-Cargo-packages situation that flag exists for. Nobody wired it up.

**Fix applied** (in worktree `fix/release-pr-refresh-lockfiles`):
1. `.github/workflows/callisto-release.yml` — pass `version_command: 'callisto version --refresh-lockfiles'` explicitly to the release action (scoped to this repo's own workflow, not the shared action's default, since that default is a public interface other consumers rely on and `cargo update --workspace` also touches third-party pins).
2. Regenerated `Cargo.lock` now, to unstick the currently-stuck release — verified a subsequent `cargo build` no longer dirties the tree.
3. Ran the release-action's 12-case contract suite: all pass.

`just ci-fast` is running now to confirm nothing else broke; I'll open the PR once it's green.
